title: An integral zero-dimensional finite-type scheme over an algebraically closed field is a point
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-algebraic-closure] and let $Z$ be an integral scheme [def-pc-integral-scheme] of finite type over $k$ [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions] with $\dim Z=0$ [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. Then the structure morphism $Z\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is an isomorphism.

source.place: Varieties, Lemma (lemma-algebraic-scheme-dim-0), tag 06LH (a zero-dimensional algebraic $k$-scheme is affine, a finite disjoint union of spectra of local Artinian $k$-algebras finite over $k$), with Algebra, Theorem 00FV (Nullstellensatz: residue fields of closed points are finite over $k$)

proof.text: $Z$ has exactly one point. $Z$ is integral, hence nonempty and irreducible [def-pc-integral-scheme]; as a topological space it is an irreducible closed subset of itself, so by [lem-weil-pbc-scheme-sober] it has a unique generic point $\eta$, $\overline{\{\eta\}}=Z$. Let $z\in Z$. The closure $\overline{\{z\}}$ is closed and irreducible (the closure of an irreducible set, here a point, is irreducible) [def-weil-irreducible-components], and $\overline{\{z\}}\subseteq Z$. If the inclusion were strict, $\overline{\{z\}}\subsetneq Z$ would be a chain of irreducible closed subsets of length $1$, so $\dim Z\ge1$ [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension], contradicting $\dim Z=0$. Hence $\overline{\{z\}}=Z$, i.e. $z$ is a generic point of $Z$, and by uniqueness $z=\eta$. So $|Z|=\{\eta\}$.

source.place: Varieties, Lemma (lemma-algebraic-scheme-dim-0), tag 06LH, second paragraph of the proof (the underlying space is discrete); written out for the irreducible case with Schemes, Lemma 01IS

proof.text:
$Z=\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $A$ a field which is a finitely generated $k$-algebra. Let $f:Z	o\operatorname{Spec}k$ be the structure morphism. As $f$ is of finite type [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions], [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], applied to the affine open $\operatorname{Spec}k$ itself, $Z=f^{-1}(\operatorname{Spec}k)$ has a cover by affine opens $\operatorname{Spec}B$ with $B$ a finitely generated $k$-algebra (via the ring map $k	o B$ for which $f|_{\operatorname{Spec}B}=\operatorname{Spec}(k	o B)$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]). Let $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ be a member containing $\eta$. $U$ is a nonempty open subset of the one-point space $Z$ (step 1), so $U=Z$ as open subscheme, i.e. $Z=\operatorname{Spec}A$ and $A=\Gamma(Z,\mathcal O_Z)$. Since $Z$ is integral and $U$ is a nonempty affine open, $A$ is an integral domain [def-pc-integral-scheme], in particular $A
eq0$. The points of $\operatorname{Spec}A$ are the prime ideals of $A$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], and there is only one, so $(0)$ (prime, since $A$ is a domain) is the only prime ideal of $A$. Then $A$ is a field: a nonzero non-unit $a\in A$ would lie in a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, which is prime and contains $a
eq0$, so $\mathfrak m
eq(0)$, a second prime ideal.

source.place: Varieties, Lemma (lemma-algebraic-scheme-dim-0), tag 06LH, first paragraph of the proof (an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $\dim A=0$) and 'a singleton scheme is affine'

proof.text: $k\to A$ is an isomorphism. $A$ is a field and a finitely generated $k$-algebra (step 2), so $A$ is a finite extension of $k$ by Zariski's lemma [lem-weil-pbc-zariski-lemma]. As $k$ is algebraically closed [def-weil-algebraic-closure], the ring map $\varphi:k\to A$ is bijective [lem-weil-pbc-alg-closed-finite-extension-trivial].

source.place: Algebra, Theorem (theorem-nullstellensatz), tag 00FV (1), as used in Varieties 06LH (finite injection $k\to A$, $\dim_kA<\infty$); then Fields, Lemma 09GR

proof.text: Conclusion. Under $Z=\operatorname{Spec}A$ (step 2) the structure morphism is $f=\operatorname{Spec}\varphi:\operatorname{Spec}A\to\operatorname{Spec}k$, $\varphi:k\to A$ the ring map of step 2 (every morphism $\operatorname{Spec}A\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is $\operatorname{Spec}$ of exactly one ring map [def-weil-affine-spectrum]). $\varphi$ is a ring isomorphism (step 3) with inverse $\varphi^{-1}$, and by functoriality of $\operatorname{Spec}$, $\operatorname{Spec}(\varphi^{-1})$ is inverse to $\operatorname{Spec}\varphi$. Hence $f$ is an isomorphism.
